Waymo LLC (/ w eɪ m oʊ/ WAY-moh) is an American autonomous driving technology company headquartered in Mountain View, California. It is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., Google's parent company. As of June 2026, Waymo operates public commercial robotaxi services in 10 US metropolitan areas, has 3,871 robotaxis in service, provides 500,000 paid rides per week, and has logged 200 million fully autonomous miles. [2] [3] [4] 

The company traces its origins to the Stanford University Racing Team, which competed in the 2005 and 2007 Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenges. [5] Google's development of self-driving technology began in January 2009, and the project was revealed in October 2010. [‡ 1] [6] [7] In December 2016, the project was renamed Waymo and spun out of Google as part of Alphabet. [‡ 2] In October 2020, Waymo became the first company to offer service to the public without safety drivers. [8] [9] [10] [11] 

Co-CEOs Tekedra Mawakana and Dmitri Dolgov have run Waymo since April 2021. [12] The company raised $11 billion in multiple outside funding rounds by 2024. In February 2026, Waymo raised $16 billion, which valued the company at $126 billion. [13] 

In January 2026, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened investigations into Waymo's robotaxis for recurring incidents of illegally passing stopped school buses, and one incident where a robotaxi hit a child who ran out from behind a parked SUV in a school zone. [14] [15] [16] 

## History

A Toyota Prius modified to operate as a Google driverless car, navigating a test course [‡ 3] (2011)

### Ground work

Google's development of self-driving technology began on January 17, 2009, [‡ 4] at Google X lab, run by Google co-founder Sergey Brin. [17] The project was launched at Google by Sebastian Thrun, the former director of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL) and Anthony Levandowski, founder of 510 Systems and Anthony's Robots. [18] [19] 

The initial software code and artificial intelligence (AI) design of the effort started before the team worked at Google, when Thrun and 15 engineers, including Dmitri Dolgov, Mike Montemerlo, Hendrik Dahlkamp, Sven Strohband, and David Stavens, built Stanley and Junior, Stanford's entries in the 2005 and 2007 DARPA Challenges. Later, aspects of this technology were used in a digital mapping project for SAIL called VuTool. [20] [21] [6] In 2007, Google acqui-hired the entire VuTool team to help advance Google's Street View technology. [20] [21] [‡ 1] [22] 

As part of Street View development, 100 Toyota Priuses [19] were outfitted with Topcon digital mapping hardware developed by 510 Systems. [23] [21] [19] 

In 2008, the Street View team launched project Ground Truth, [24] to create accurate road maps by extracting data from satellites and street views. [25] 

### Pribot

In February 2008, a Discovery Channel producer for the documentary series Prototype This! phoned Levandowski. [21] [26] The producer requested to borrow Levandowski's Ghost Rider, the autonomous two-wheeled motorcycle Levandowski's Berkeley team had built for the 2004 DARPA Grand Challenge [5] that Levandowski had later donated to the Smithsonian. [27] Since the motorcycle was not available, Levandowski offered to retrofit a Toyota Prius as a self-driving pizza delivery car for the show. [21] 

As a Google employee, Levandowski asked Larry Page and Thrun whether Google wanted to participate in the show. Both declined, citing liability issues. [5] However, they authorized Levandowski to move forward with the project, as long as it was not associated with Google. [21] [28] Within weeks Levandowski founded Anthony's Robots to do so. [20] He retrofitted the car with light detection and ranging (lidar) technology, sensors, and cameras. The Stanford team behind the Stanley car provided the project with its codebase. [5] The ensuing episode depicting Pribot delivering pizza across the San Francisco Bay Bridge under police escort aired in December 2008. [29] [18] [28] [30] 

The project's success convinced Google to greenlight its own self-driving car program in January 2009. [5] In 2011, Google acquired 510 Systems (co-founded by Levandowski, Pierre-Yves Droz and Andrew Schultz), and Anthony's Robots for an estimated US$20 million. [23] [20] [29] [18] [31] Levandowski's vehicle and hardware, and Stanford's AI technology and software, became the nucleus of the project. [5] 

A Firefly self-driving Waymo car (2017)

### Project Chauffeur

After almost two years of road testing with seven vehicles, the New York Times revealed Google's project on October 9, 2010. [6] Google announced its initiative later the same day. [7] 

Starting in 2010, lawmakers in various states expressed concerns over how to regulate autonomous vehicles. A related Nevada law went into effect on March 1, 2012. [32] Google had been lobbying for such laws. [33] [34] [35] A modified Prius was licensed by the Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) in May 2012. The car was "driven" by Chris Urmson with Levandowski in the passenger seat. [36] This was the first US license for a self-driven car. [32] 

 In January 2014 [37] Google was granted a patent for a transportation service funded by advertising that included autonomous vehicles as a transport method. [38] In late May, Google revealed an autonomous prototype, which had no steering wheel, gas pedal, or brake pedal. [‡ 5] [39] In December, Google unveiled a Firefly prototype that was planned to be tested on San Francisco Bay Area roads beginning in early 2015. [40] [41] 

A self-driving car with the previous Google branding (2016)

In 2015, Levandowski left the project. In August 2015, Google hired former Hyundai Motor executive, John Krafcik, as CEO. [42] In fall 2015, the first ride in a fully autonomous vehicle by a non-Google employee was undertaken by a blind man in Austin, Texas. It was the first entirely autonomous trip on a public road and was not accompanied by a test driver or police escort. [43] [44] The car had no steering wheel or floor pedals. [45] By the end of 2015, Project Chauffeur vehicles had driven more than one million miles. [23] 

Google spent $1.1 billion on the project between 2009 and 2015. For comparison, the acquisition of Cruise Automation by General Motors in March 2016 was for $500 million, and Uber's acquisition of Otto in August 2016 was for $680 million. [46] 

### Waymo

In May 2016, Google and Stellantis announced an order of 100 Chrysler Pacifica hybrid minivans to test the self-driving technology. [47] In December 2016, the project changed its name to Waymo and spun out of Google as part of Alphabet. [‡ 2] The name was derived from "a new way forward in mobility". [48] In May 2016, the company opened a 53,000-square-foot (4,900 m 2) technology center in Novi, Michigan. [‡ 6] 

In February 2017, Waymo sued Uber and its subsidiary self-driving trucking company, Otto, alleging trade secret theft and patent infringement. The company claimed that three ex-Google employees, including Anthony Levandowski, had stolen trade secrets, including thousands of files, from Google before joining Uber. [49] The alleged infringement was related to Waymo's proprietary lidar technology, [50] [51] Google accused Uber of colluding with Levandowski. [52] Levandowski allegedly downloaded 9 gigabytes of data that included over a hundred trade secrets; eight of which were at stake during the trial. [53] [54] An ensuing settlement gave Waymo 0.34% of Uber stock, [49] the equivalent of $245 million. Uber agreed not to infringe Waymo's intellectual property. [55] Part of the agreement included a guarantee that "Waymo confidential information is not being incorporated in Uber Advanced Technologies Group hardware and software." [56] In statements released after the settlement, Uber maintained that it received no trade secrets. [57] In May, according to an Uber spokesman, Uber had fired Levandowski, which resulted in the loss of roughly $250 million of his equity in Uber, which almost exactly equaled the settlement. [49] Uber announced that it was halting production of self-driving trucks through Otto in July 2018, and the subsidiary company was shuttered. [58] In 2020, Levandowski pled guilty to one of 33 charges, and was sentenced to 18 months in prison. [59] 

Waymo began testing minivans without a safety driver on public roads in Chandler, Arizona, in October 2017. [60] In 2017, Waymo unveiled new sensors and chips that are less expensive to manufacture, cameras that improve visibility, and wipers to clear the lidar system. [61] At the beginning of the self-driving car program, they used a $75,000 lidar system from Velodyne. [62] In 2017, the cost decreased approximately 90 percent, as Waymo converted to in-house built lidar. [63] Waymo has applied its technology to various cars including the Prius, Audi TT, Chrysler Pacifica, and Lexus RX450h. [64] [65] Waymo partners with Lyft on pilot projects and product development. [66] 

Waymo started testing in Phoenix without safety drivers in November 2017. [67] 

Waymo-operated Jaguar I-Pace in San Francisco (2023)

In March 2018, Jaguar Land Rover announced that Waymo had ordered up to 20,000 of its I-Pace electric SUVs at an estimated cost of more than $1 billion. [68] [69] In late May 2018, Alphabet announced plans to add up to 62,000 Pacifica Hybrid minivans to the fleet. [70] [71] Also in May 2018, Waymo established Huimo Business Consulting subsidiary in Shanghai. [72] 

In October 2018, the California Department of Motor Vehicles issued a permit for Waymo to operate cars without safety drivers. Waymo was the first company to receive a permit for day and night testing on public roads and highways. Waymo announced that its service would include Mountain View, Sunnyvale, Los Altos, and Palo Alto. [73] In July 2019, Waymo received permission to transport passengers. [74] 

In December 2018, Waymo launched Waymo One in Phoenix, transporting passengers. The service used safety drivers to monitor some rides, with others provided in select areas without them. In November 2019, Waymo One became the first autonomous service worldwide to operate without safety drivers. [75] [11] [76] Waymo One launched in San Francisco, beginning with a "trusted tester" rollout. [77] In March 2022, Waymo began offering rides for Waymo staff in San Francisco without a safety driver. [78] 

In April 2019, Waymo announced plans for vehicle assembly in Detroit at the former American Axle & Manufacturing plant, bringing between 100 and 400 jobs to the area. Waymo used vehicle assembler Magna to turn Jaguar I-PACE electric SUVs and Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid minivans into Waymo Level 4 autonomous vehicles. [79] [80] Waymo subsequently reverted to retrofitting existing models rather than a custom design. [81]
